title: Unique invariant measures versus cellular-automaton ergodicity
formal: Does uniqueness of the invariant Borel probability measure of a deterministic cellular automaton imply convergence of every initial probability distribution to that measure? Already on the one-dimensional full shift, the implication in question is \[\bigl(\exists!\pi\in\mathcal P(A^{\mathbb Z}),\ F_*\pi=\pi\bigr)\ \Longrightarrow\ \bigl(\forall\mu\in\mathcal P(A^{\mathbb Z}),\ (F^n)_*\mu\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{\mathrm{weak}}\pi\bigr).\] The quantifier ranges over every finite nonempty alphabet \(A\), every finite radius and every deterministic local rule. The published answer is negative: Törmä constructs a one-dimensional automaton with a unique invariant measure which fails this convergence requirement.

source_formulation.text: For deterministic cellular automata, does having exactly one invariant Borel probability measure force weak convergence to it from every initial distribution?
source_formulation.caption: Editorial paraphrase of the historical implication question

why: The question distinguishes a unique statistical equilibrium from convergence toward that equilibrium at each time. Cellular automata add strong locality and translation symmetry to general compact dynamical systems, so the failure of the implication is a substantive structural result. It shows that these restrictions still permit persistent sparse activity invisible to the unique invariant distribution.
status_note: Resolved negatively by Törmä, Journal of Computer and System Sciences 81(2) (2015), Theorem 9.1 (Theorem 37 in arXiv:1310.0670v2). The constructed one-dimensional deterministic full-shift automaton is uniquely ergodic but not nilpotent; by Theorem 3.3 of the original STACS 2011 source it is not Markov-theoretically ergodic. The exact model and invariant-measure conventions were checked on 16 September 2026; no Lean formalization is claimed.

importance.reason: A resolved foundational separation between two inequivalent notions of ergodicity for local deterministic dynamics, established by a technically substantial one-dimensional construction.

sentences: A deterministic cellular automaton can have exactly one invariant probability distribution without every initial distribution converging to it.
The historical question asks whether locality and translation symmetry force these two notions of ergodicity to coincide.
Törmä’s published one-dimensional construction is uniquely ergodic, with the all-blank point mass as its invariant measure, but is not nilpotent.
The original source proves that Markov-theoretic convergence on the integer line would imply nilpotency, so the construction answers the question negatively.
The card is archived as resolved, distinguishing the published theorem from a complete Lean formalization of its proof.

definitions: A configuration is any function \(x:\mathbb Z\to A\), with no periodicity, finite-support or random-input restriction. Fix \(r\in\mathbb N\) and a finite rule table \(f:A^{\{-r,\ldots,r\}}\to A\). The global map applies it synchronously, \(F(x)_i=f((x_{i+j})_{-r\le j\le r})\). Give \(A\) the discrete topology and \(A^{\mathbb Z}\) the product topology. A cylinder \([p]\) prescribes a pattern \(p:D\to A\) on a finite set \(D\subset\mathbb Z\). The Borel sets are generated by these cylinders; \(\mathcal P\) denotes all countably additive Borel probability measures. Pushforward is \(F_*\mu(E)=\mu(F^{-1}(E))\), and invariance means equality on all Borel sets. In particular the invariant measures need not be invariant under spatial shifts. Weak convergence here is equivalent to \((F^n)_*\mu([p])\to\pi([p])\) for every finite pattern. The source calls uniqueness alone symbolic-dynamical unique ergodicity, and uniqueness together with the displayed convergence Markov-theoretic ergodicity. These are the meanings used on this card. A state \(q\in A\) is quiescent if the constant configuration \(q^{\mathbb Z}\) is fixed. An automaton is nilpotent if some \(q\) and some uniform \(N\in\mathbb N\) satisfy \(F^N(x)=q^{\mathbb Z}\) for every configuration \(x\). No rate of convergence, effective representation of arbitrary measures, numerical tolerance or computational time bound is requested. A one-dimensional counterexample also refutes a broader universal implication allowing other lattices.
answer_criterion: The historical implication is resolved negatively in the literature. A complete Lean formalization must construct a finite alphabet and finite local rule, prove that exactly one invariant Borel probability measure exists, and exhibit an initial probability measure whose iterated pushforwards fail to converge weakly to it. It may instead prove the exact one-dimensional equivalence between Markov-theoretic ergodicity and nilpotency and combine it with a formalized uniquely ergodic, non-nilpotent construction. All construction and measure-theoretic claims used in that argument must be checked; a citation or an assertion of non-nilpotency alone is not a Lean proof. This editorial review does not claim such a formalization has been supplied.

context_blocks.text: A single invariant measure describes the possible equilibrium distribution. Convergence asks more: every starting distribution must approach that equilibrium under repeated updates, without replacing the sequence by averages over time. This distinction is essential in deterministic dynamics.

The original source defines the convergence requirement in §2.6. Its Theorem 3.3 proves that for deterministic cellular automata on the integer line this requirement is equivalent to nilpotency. Nilpotency imposes a common finite time after which every configuration has become the same constant configuration.

Törmä’s journal theorem constructs a finite-rule, one-dimensional automaton which is uniquely ergodic but not nilpotent. Its unique invariant probability measure is concentrated on the completely blank configuration. The automaton is therefore a counterexample in the deterministic full-shift model of the question.

The author manuscript states a parameterized construction: the automaton is always non-nilpotent and is uniquely ergodic exactly when its effective parameter set is infinite. Choosing the natural numbers as that set supplies the required instance. The journal labels the main result Theorem 9.1, whereas the checked manuscript labels it Theorem 37.

Combining the construction with the source’s nilpotency characterization proves failure of Markov-theoretic ergodicity. Equivalently, asymptotic nilpotency on the integer line would force nilpotency, so some configuration has a cell that is nonblank at arbitrarily late times. The corresponding point-mass distribution cannot converge cylinderwise to the all-blank point mass.

This resolution uses neither probabilistic updates nor a restriction to spatially invariant initial measures. Those conventions would change the question. The result is recorded as a published mathematical resolution, with the archival decision separate from the stronger requirement of a fully checked Lean proof.
